name.value: Food cue reactivity in NAcc predicts subsequent snack intake

spans.text: ### Food cue reactivity in NAcc predicts subsequent snack intake

definition.value: Activation in the left NAcc to food vs. non-food cues showed a significant correlation with subsequent crisp consumption.

spans.text: As predicted, activation in the left NAcc to food vs. non-food cues showed a significant correlation with subsequent crisp consumption (Rs = .47, p = 0.019; 95% confidence intervals (CI) 0.09– 0.73, ) [right NAcc not significant, Rs = .31, p = 0.13; CI = − 0.1– 0.63] but no correlation with physiological craving state (Rs = .129; CI = − 0.28– 0.5), trait loss of control over food intake (Rs = .02; CI = − 0.38– 0.41), or with specific ratings of crisp wanting or liking (Rs = .2 and Rs = .21; CI − 0.2–0.56) (all p's > 0.3).

name.value: NAcc food cue reactivity interacts with self-control to predict BMI

spans.text: ### NAcc food cue reactivity interacts with self-control to predict BMI

definition.value: Food-related self-control interacted with neural responses in the left NAcc to predict BMI.

spans.text: Moderated multiple regression analysis indicated that food-related self-control interacted with neural responses in the left NAcc to predict BMI (t = 3.35, p = 0.0031; ∆ R 2 = 0.3).

value: Participants who reported high levels of loss of control over food intake (i.e. low self-control) showed a positive correlation between neural cue reactivity in the left NAcc and BMI, where as those with strong self-control with respect to food intake showed a negative correlation

spans.text: Participants who reported high levels of loss of control over food intake (i.e. low self-control) showed a positive correlation between neural cue reactivity in the left NAcc and BMI, where as those with strong self-control with respect to food intake showed a negative correlation ( ).

Participants who reported high levels of loss of control over food intake (i.e. low self-control) showed a positive correlation between neural cue reactivity in the left NAcc and BMI, where as those with strong self-control with respect to food intake showed a negative correlation

The interaction between NAcc responses to food cues and self-control in predicting BMI supports recent ‘dual hit’ models, which argue that vulnerability to overweight is conferred by two orthogonal, interacting traits: increased food reward sensitivity (incentive salience) and the propensity to loss of intentional control over behaviour.

Whilst food cue reactivity in the NAcc was not directly associated with BMI, there was a positive relationship between NAcc activation and BMI in individuals reporting a high loss of control over food intake.
